notes.text: For more than 4, sear the salmon in two batches so the pieces have room, and keep the first batch on the plate under foil.

move.title: Boil it down to a glaze
move.body: Reducing means letting a liquid bubble until some of its water steams away, so it gets thicker and stronger. Today you'll boil pineapple juice, soy sauce, and brown sugar down into a shiny teriyaki glaze, sear salmon in a hot pan, and spoon the glaze over the top.

callback.body: In honey-garlic chicken you watched a sauce bubble down until the bubbles turned big, slow, and sticky. A teriyaki glaze works the same way. This time it bubbles in its own pan while the salmon cooks.

why.title: Why it thickens
why.body: Pineapple juice and soy sauce are mostly water. As they bubble, the water leaves as steam and the sugar stays behind, so the sauce gets thicker, darker, and sweeter. A spoon tells you: when the glaze coats the back of it, it's ready.

why.title: It thickens more as it cools
why.body: A glaze that looks a little thin in the hot pan sets up as it cools on the salmon. Stop when it coats the spoon. If you wait until it's thick in the pan, it turns sticky like candy on the plate.

why.title: Dry fish browns
why.body: Water on the outside of the salmon has to boil away before the fish can brown. Patting it dry with paper towels lets a golden crust start right away, and a crusted piece lets go of the pan instead of sticking.

why.title: Leave it alone
why.body: Salmon sticks to the pan at first. Once a crust forms, it lets go by itself. Poke it too early and it tears. Wait, and it slides when you nudge it.

wrong.sign: The glaze is thin and watery
wrong.fix: Keep it bubbling a few more minutes, stirring now and then, until it coats the back of a spoon.

wrong.sign: The glaze is thick and sticky like candy
wrong.fix: It bubbled too long. Stir in a spoonful of water at a time over low heat until it loosens.

wrong.sign: The salmon is stuck to the pan
wrong.fix: Wait another minute. When the crust forms, it lets go. Slide a thin spatula under it slowly.
Put the lid on the skillet and cook 1 to 2 more minutes on medium-low, then check again.

quiz.q: What happens to a sauce when it reduces?
choices: Water steams away and it gets thicker
quiz.explain: Bubbling lets water escape as steam, so what stays behind is thicker and stronger.

choices: When it coats the back of a spoon
quiz.explain: It keeps thickening as it cools, so stop when it coats the spoon.

steps.text: Put the rice in the medium saucepan and cover it with cold water. Swish it with your hand, then carefully pour off the cloudy water, holding the rice back with your hand. Do this 3 times.
steps.tip: Rinsing washes off loose starch, so the rice cooks up fluffy instead of gluey.

steps.text: Add {qty:water} of water to the rice. Bring it to a boil over high heat with the lid off. Then turn the heat to low, put the lid on, and cook without lifting the lid.
steps.tip: When the timer rings, turn off the burner and leave the lid on. The rice keeps steaming while you finish.

steps.text: Open the pineapple and pour it into the colander set over the small bowl, so the juice runs into the bowl. Keep the chunks in the colander for later.
steps.tip: Keep your fingers away from the cut edge of the lid. It's as sharp as a knife.

steps.text: Peel the garlic. Scrape the skin off the ginger with the edge of the spoon. Grate them both on the small holes of the grater.
steps.tip: The pieces get small fast. Stop before your fingers get near the holes.

steps.text: Pour the pineapple juice into the small saucepan. Add the soy sauce, brown sugar, rice vinegar, garlic, and ginger, and stir. Bring it to a boil over medium heat, then let it bubble, stirring now and then, until it coats the back of the spoon.
steps.look: Glossy, darker, and thick enough to coat the spoon.
steps.tip: Bubbling sugar is hotter than boiling water. Keep your hands back and stir with a long spoon.

steps.text: Turn off the heat under the glaze and leave it on the burner.
Lay the salmon on the plate and pat every side dry with paper towels. Sprinkle it with {qty:salt} salt.
Throw the paper towels away. Wash your hands with soap, and wipe anything the raw salmon or its package touched.
Heat the oil in the skillet over medium-high heat until it shimmers.
Use the tongs to lay the salmon in the pan, rounded side down, laying each piece down away from you. Put the tongs in the sink, and don't use them again for cooked food.
Wash your hands, and put the raw-salmon plate in the sink. From here on, use the clean spatula.
Leave the salmon alone while the bottom browns. Don't poke it or move it.
steps.look: A golden crust, and the piece slides when you nudge it.

steps.text: Turn the heat down to medium. Gently flip each piece with the spatula and cook the other side.
steps.tip: Flip it away from you, so any spatter goes the other way.

steps.text: Slide the thermometer into the side of the thickest piece. It needs to read at least 145°F. If it doesn't, cook 1 more minute and check again.
Move the salmon to a clean plate with the spatula. Tip the pineapple chunks into the skillet and stir them until they are warm and browned in spots.

Turn off the stove. Fluff the rice with the fork. Serve the salmon on the rice with the pineapple, spoon the glaze over the top, and sprinkle with green onions and the sesame seeds if you're using them.
steps.tip: The handle stays hot for a long time. Leave an oven mitt on it so nobody grabs it bare-handed.
